extracted.intended_audience: criminalists, trial lawyers, judges, and forensic examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on conducting and evaluating witness testimony and judicial/forensic inference in criminal trials, including persuasion, presentation of evidence, and diagnosing mistaken inferences. Emphasizes psychological observation, the sequencing of evidence, and methods to test inferred vs perceived facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize examiner eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner... must meet his witness with the least conceivable use of eloquence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eloquence by the examiner can sugestively implant the examiner's theories in the witness; to avoid having the witness adopt the examiner's point of view, use minimal rhetorical influence. This is especially important with uneducated witnesses who are more suggestible; educated witnesses or some women are less susceptible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for forensic persuasion on juries
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches of the prosecution and defense are the most important things in the trial... the question of guilt or innocence does not depend upon the number and weight of the testimony but upon the more or less skilful interpretation of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that juries are strongly influenced by oratory and interpretation of evidence; legal actors should craft addresses that reproduce evidence intelligibly for jurors. The danger is that persuasiveness appeals to imagination and affections rather than deliberative understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw the brief (order and presentation of evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination of the chronological order in which to present evidence, i.e., the drawing of the brief... If the brief is well drawn, everything develops logically and psychologically in a good way and the case goes on well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful sequencing of evidence (chronology/brief) is an artistic and central task; a poorly drawn brief produces irrelevance and confusion for a jury. Preparing the brief requires deliberate planning and intelligence; if done effectively it reduces reliance on oratorical persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge as psychologist to monitor jury influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The only help against this is in the study by the presiding justice, not as lawyer but as psychologist, of the faces of the jury... He must observe very narrowly and carefully every influence exercised by the speeches, which is irrelevant to the real problem, and then in summing up call it to the attention of the jury and bring them back to the proper point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presiding judges should watch jurors for irrelevant persuasion effects and correct them in summing-up. This requires acute psychological observation and an ability to identify when speeches have diverted jurors from the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know theories and tricks of persuadability
rubrics_metrics.description: Nowadays persuadability is hardly more studied but anybody who has empirically attained some proficiency in it has acquired the same tricks that are taught by theory... Hence the study of the proper authors can not be too much recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study classical and modern rhetorical and psychological works (Aristotle, Cicero, etc.) to recognize persuasion techniques and to counteract them in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish perception from inference
rubrics_metrics.description: The witness may have 'seen' a watch... when in reality he has only heard a noise that he took for the ticking of a watch and hence inferred that there had really been a watch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always probe whether a witness actually perceived an event (saw/heard/smelled) or merely inferred it. Systematically question the source and chain of inference to reveal mistaken beliefs that witness treats as perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require witness to report how they inferred
rubrics_metrics.description: There would be little difficulty if people told us how they had inferred, for then a test by means of careful questions would be easy enough--but they do not tell...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elicit the explicit sequence of inferences that led to a witness's belief; test each premise. If the witness omits their inferential steps, reconstruct them by questioning to expose weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against hasty inference from insufficient premises
rubrics_metrics.description: A hasty inference from insufficient premises may be much more comfortable than more careful observation and study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of rapid conclusions based on limited data; press for fuller observation or corroboration rather than accepting convenient inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for verbal associations driving judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal associations have a considerable share... If we see the thing watch, we get the word watch... the occurrence does not leave him with the word merely, there is a direct inference 'B has tuberculosis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that words and concepts can trigger automatic inferences; separate the linguistic/labeling moment from the factual basis. Question witnesses to determine whether a term arose from a full perceptual basis or from association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust for inferential leaps due to character or training
rubrics_metrics.description: In every inference there are leaps made by each inferer according to his character and training... people inclined to mathematics make the greatest leaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the witness's background and cognitive style when evaluating their inferential leaps; what seems obvious to one (e.g., a mathematician) may be an unjustified leap in ordinary matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware witnesses who substitute forms/images for detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Witnesses who have a certain sense of form... their inferential leaps consists in their omitting the detailed expression and in inserting the notion of form instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a witness reports a composite 'image' rather than discrete observations, test alternative explanations (e.g., reversed sequence, self-actions, multiple actors). The vividness of an imagined composite can mask unreliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review sequence of inferences that produced impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary in any case to review the sequence of inferences which led to this impression and to examine their correctness. Unfortunately the witness is rarely aware whether he has perceived or merely inferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace back from the witness's final impression to each contributing observation or assumption; test the truth and relevance of each link. This is essential because impressions often rest on untested inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never accept a claim of impossibility without probing alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Hence the rule that a witness's assertion that a thing is impossible must never be trusted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a witness asserts that some scenario 'cannot' have occurred, ask for the reasons and explore other eventualities (unlikely routes, tools, third parties). Demonstrate overlooked possibilities to undermine unwarranted certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek historical truth via mass of details, not mathematical truth
rubrics_metrics.description: We criminalists 'must not dally with mathematical truth but must seek historical truth. We start with a mass of details, unite them, and succeed by means of this union and test in attaining a result which permits us to judge the existence and the characteristics of past events.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on collecting, uniting, and testing many small facts to reconstruct past events; avoid overreliance on abstract mathematical certainty disconnected from historical particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate inferences using similarity and associative connection (Humean test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hume's two propositions: (1) I have found that such an object has always been attended with such an effect. (2) I foresee that other objects which are in appearance similar, will be attended with similar effects... The criminological importance... the correctness of our inferences depends upon its discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the present case is legitimately similar to prior cases used as basis for inference; make explicit the associative link that connects premises to conclusion rather than assuming it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize improbable or 'round' numerical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: We are generally inclined to consider an inference wrong which indicates that accidental matters have occurred in regular numerical relation... people are shy of naming such 'improbable ratios'... bankers find that tickets with 'pretty numbers' are difficult to sell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither automatically distrust round numbers nor accept them unexamined; both round (suspiciously neat) and irregular figures deserve scrutiny and corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value breadth of associations when judging correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of probability of a judgment’s correctness depends upon the richness of the field of the associations brought to bear in establishing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage expansive associative thinking and wide knowledge when forming judgments: richer associative networks provide better grounds for correct inferences; avoid narrow legal knowledge alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate numerical majority with correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a judgment has been made by a single judge or is the verdict of any number of jurymen is quite indifferent since the correctness of a judgment does not lie in numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate minority opinions carefully; a lone voice may be correct despite majority disagreement. Beware conformity, dependent testimony, and shared sources of error among many witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess manuscripts by purpose, sources, personality, and external form
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily some clearness may be attained by paying attention to the purpose of the manuscript, especially in order to ascertain its sources and the personality of the writer... The purposiveness, order, and continuity of a manuscript indicate that it was not written after the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating written records, consider why it was written, who wrote it, source material, and physical/formal features (order, continuity) to judge whether it is contemporaneous and reliable rather than post hoc fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and guard against five types of mistaken inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Such mistakes may be classified under five heads: (1) Aprioristic mistakes. (Natural prejudices). (2) Mistakes in observation. (3) Mistakes in generalization. (When the facts are right and the inferences wrong). (4) Mistakes of confusion. (Ambiguity of terms or mistakes by association). (5) Logical fallacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically consider each class when evaluating testimony: check for ingrained prejudices, observational errors, unwarranted generalizations, ambiguous language/associations, and formal logical errors. All five are common in trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch fixed sensory prejudices that resist reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The prejudices arising from sensation... are therefore very difficult to destroy... Such fixed impressions we meet in every criminal trial, and if once we have considered how the criminal had committed a crime we no longer get free of the impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify strong sensory-based impressions (first impressions, vivid perceptions) that persist despite contrary evidence; deliberately counteract them by re-evaluation and testing of premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about inferences from environmental/contextual cues (mistakes in generalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under mistakes of generalization the most important processes are those of arrangement, where the environment or accompanying circumstances exercise so determinative an influence that the inference is often made from them alone... e.g., the Tanagra in the house of an art-connoisseur I take to be genuine without further examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid leaping from context/association to conclusions about an object or event; require direct evidence rather than relying solely on circumstantial or environmental cues which often reflect prejudice or routine expectations.
